claims.text: The proposed starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase, disordered, equiatomic solid solution containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
The degree of inherent lattice distortion controls superconducting behavior in disordered multi-element HEAs.
Lattice distortion affects superconductivity by modulating electron-phonon coupling strength.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch increases lattice distortion.
Elemental substitution can vary atomic-size mismatch while overall electron count is kept similar.
Arc melting, homogenization, and controlled cooling are compatible with obtaining a single-phase solid-solution alloy.
Using identical processing conditions makes lattice distortion the main source of differences in superconducting properties.
Lattice strain measurements or deviations in lattice parameters can quantify the proposed lattice-distortion mediator.
Large lattice distortion increases electron scattering.
Large lattice distortion and associated scattering perturb phonon modes.
The perturbation of phonon modes reduces net electron-phonon coupling strength.
Reduced electron-phonon coupling lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
A high-distortion HEA will have a lower superconducting transition temperature than a low-distortion baseline HEA.
Greater lattice distortion may alter superconducting gap parameters or coherence length.
Choosing baseline constituent elements with similar atomic radii produces relatively low lattice distortion.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to single-phase, disordered solid-solution HEAs with similar electron counts.
Multiphase or partly ordered structures and significant magnetic interactions may limit applicability of the proposed mechanism.
Changes in density of states and nonlinear electron-phonon coupling could compensate for scattering effects and obscure a quantitative distortion–Tc relationship.
X-ray diffraction, resistivity, and magnetic susceptibility measurements are proposed to compare distortion and superconducting transition temperatures across the controlled series.
Failure to observe a systematic decrease in Tc with increasing measured distortion would falsify the stated distortion-controlled Tc trend.
